report:
# Does Hypnosis Help with Smoking Cessation? A Mixed but Cautiously Positive Picture

The evidence is more nuanced than a simple "yes." The most rigorous evaluation—the **Cochrane systematic review** (updated through 2019–2024)—found **insufficient evidence** to conclude that hypnotherapy is more effective than other cessation methods or no treatment at all, largely due to high risk of bias and methodological weaknesses across the included trials ([cochranelibrary.com](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub4/full), [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20927723/)).

However, more recent and broader analyses lean supportive. A 2025 systematic review by Ekanayake and Elkins, covering 63 studies from 1968–2022, reported **positive support** for hypnosis in smoking cessation, taking a wider lens than Cochrane's narrower trial inclusion criteria ([ishhypnosis.org](https://www.ishhypnosis.org/encyclopedia/the-potential-benefit-of-hypnosis-for-smoking-cessation/)). A 2025 Tandfonline systematic review similarly concluded that "the efficacy of hypnotherapy for smoking cessation is positive," while noting more studies with biologically confirmed abstinence are needed ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00207144.2024.2434082)).

A 2023 Frontiers meta-analytic overview offers a middle ground: of six effects reported across five reviews (including three Cochrane reviews), effect sizes ranged from d=0.12 to d=0.84, but **only two of six were statistically significant** ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1330238/full)).

**Bottom line:** The strongest, most methodologically rigorous evidence (Cochrane) does not confirm hypnosis definitively outperforms other quit methods, largely due to poor trial quality. Newer, broader reviews suggest a plausible positive effect, but the overall evidence base remains inconsistent and limited by weak study designs. The honest answer is "possibly, but not conclusively proven"—not a clear "yes."
